plan.title: Stochastic gradient descent on a loss surface
plan.description: An oval bowl-shaped surface stands for a model's loss (its error for each pair of weight values), lowest at the centre. An orange ball takes stochastic gradient descent steps: each uses a noisy downhill estimate, as if from a small random batch of data, so its trail zig-zags. A grey ghost ball starts at the same place and takes exact gradient descent steps for comparison. Change step size and batch size and watch the orange path wander, speed up or overshoot, and how wide its jitter cloud near the minimum gets.
plan.reason: Stochastic gradient descent is easiest to understand by comparing its noisy path with exact descent on the same surface while you change step size and batch size and watch the results.

parameters.label: Show this step's noisy gradient arrow

interactions: Press play or step once. Each step moves both balls by one update, for up to 200 steps.
Before running, drag the orange start ball to any point on the surface. The ghost ball starts from the same point.
Raise the learning rate: steps get longer, the path crosses the narrow direction of the bowl and zig-zags, and the final jitter cloud gets wider.
Raise the batch size: the noise shrinks, so the orange path gets smoother and closer to the ghost's path. At batch size 1 it is at its noisiest.
Readouts show the step count, the orange ball's loss, the ghost's loss and the current noise size.
assumptions: Illustration: the surface is a simple made-up bowl, not a model trained on real data, and the batch noise is simulated.
Loss is 0.5·(x² + 4y²), so the bowl is four times steeper across than along, with the minimum at the centre.

Each stochastic step uses the true slope plus random noise (from a fixed seed). The noise is on average zero, and its size is a fixed amount divided by the square root of the batch size, which mimics averaging over that many samples.
Each step moves against the noisy gradient: new position = old position − learning rate × noisy gradient. The arrow shows the noisy gradient, and the ball moves the opposite way.
The ghost ball uses the exact gradient with the same learning rate and no noise.
The run stops after 200 steps or when you pause.
The trail draws one marker every 2 steps, at most 100 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.
Single stochastic steps can raise the loss. The orange ball goes downhill on average, not on every step.
With a fixed learning rate, the orange ball never settles exactly at the minimum. It keeps jittering in a cloud near the centre. The cloud shrinks with a smaller learning rate or a bigger batch.
The learning rate stops at 0.45, below 0.5, the value where exact descent on this bowl would bounce out of control. Fast oscillation is visible near the top of the range, but not runaway divergence.
Real loss surfaces have many dimensions, flat regions and multiple dips. This two-weight bowl shows only the core idea.
plan.learningGoal: See that stochastic gradient descent follows noisy downhill estimates. It goes downhill on average but not on every step. A larger batch reduces the noise, and the learning rate trades speed against overshoot and jitter near the minimum.

draft.title: Stochastic gradient descent vs exact descent on a loss bowl
draft.description: An oval bowl-shaped surface shows a made-up loss over two weights: gentle left to right, steep into the view, lowest at the centre (small dark dot). An orange ball takes stochastic gradient descent steps with a noisy gradient and leaves a thick orange zig-zag trail. A see-through blue ghost ball takes exact gradient descent steps from the same start, with a thin pale blue trail. A purple arrow on the orange ball shows this step's noisy gradient; the ball moves the opposite way. A small orange pin marks the start.

parameters.label: Show this step's noisy gradient arrow

assumptions: Illustration: the surface is a simple made-up bowl, not a model trained on real data, and the batch noise is simulated.
Loss = 0.5·(a² + 4b²). a runs across the view (gentle) and b runs into it (four times steeper). The minimum is at the centre. The surface is drawn at 0.1 × loss, and the readouts show the true loss.

Noisy gradient = true gradient + random noise from a fixed seed. The noise averages zero, and its sd per slope component is 1.5/√(batch size). Update: new = old − learning rate × noisy gradient. The ghost uses the exact gradient with the same rate.

The purple arrow is this step's noisy gradient, drawn at 0.5 × its true length (one fixed scale). The ball moves the opposite way, scaled by the learning rate. Very short arrows near the minimum may be too small to draw.

Drag the orange ball to set its start along the steep direction, and the small orange start pin to set it along the gentle direction. The ghost always starts from the same point. Dragging starts a fresh run.

Each run is at most 200 steps, 10 per second. The trails draw one marker every 2 steps (at most 100) plus the current position; every step still runs. Single SGD steps can raise the loss: it falls on average, not on every step.

With a fixed rate, SGD keeps jittering near the minimum. The rate stops at 0.45, below the 0.5 where exact descent on this bowl would diverge. A step that would leave the drawn surface stops at its edge.

findings.message: At the start the orange SGD ball and the grey ghost have the same position and the same radius, so only the grey sphere shows. The 'SGD' label points at a grey ball and the orange ball cannot be seen. Make the ghost smaller or translucent, or offset it, so both balls show.

The plan says to drag the orange start ball to any point and have the ghost start from the same point. Instead the orange ball drags only across (x), and the start along the bowl is set by dragging the grey ghost (z). Let the orange ball drag freely over the surface and have the ghost follow its start.
The plan's limitation describes 100 markers, one every 2 steps. The artifact marks every step instead. This is disclosed, but the plan and artifact disagree.

The trace shows the noisy-gradient arrow hidden (length 0.21, shorter than its 0.4 head), so the promised arrow disappears once the ball nears the minimum. That is where noise matters most. The 0.15 scale is too small. Use a larger single disclosed scale so the arrow stays visible at true proportion.

The grey exact-descent trail mostly lies under the thick orange trail and the balls, so the learner cannot compare the two paths. Draw the ghost trail more distinctly (contrasting colour, slight lift or thickness) and keep the ghost ball distinct from the orange one.
At learning rate 0.45 the trace shows the noisy-gradient arrow hidden (length 0.11), so the step's gradient cannot be seen. The arrow scale is too small.

The dense orange zig-zag hides both the orange and the grey ball near the centre, and the grey ghost trail can hardly be told apart. The 'SGD' and 'Exact GD' labels float over a tangle. Thin or fade older trail segments and make the balls stand out above the trail.
The low end of the learning rate and the batch-size extremes (1 and 64) were not sampled, so the promised smoothing at large batch size was not verified.
The side view confirms that the orange SGD ball is hidden inside the grey ghost at the start, so it is missing from the picture.
The noisy-gradient arrow is hidden in this running state because it is shorter than its head. The promised per-step arrow is missing.
The grey ghost trail cannot be seen next to the orange trail, so the path comparison is lost.

findings.message: Default framing: the steep, tall walls (up to 3.75 high at the corners) make the bowl a narrow U that fills only the middle third of the frame, with wide empty margins on both sides. The region where SGD actually moves and jitters (near the centre) takes up a small patch of the image. Use a lower vertical scale K, or a higher, closer camera, so the area around the minimum fills the view.
The plan says the trail shows one marker every 2 steps (at most 100). The artifact draws every step (up to 201 points) and says so in its assumptions. This is harmless, but it differs from the plan.

The exact-GD trail is twice as thick (0.045 vs 0.022) and is drawn 0.1 above the surface while the SGD trail is at 0.03, so the dark blue path sits on top of the thin orange SGD path and hides most of it. The noisy zig-zag the lesson is about is only visible in small fragments. Draw the SGD trail thicker and on top, and make the ghost trail thinner, lighter or lower.

The whole run after 27 steps fits in a small patch near the bottom centre of the frame, so the trail and the jitter near the minimum are hard to read at this scale. This is the same framing problem as in the default view.

At learning rate 0.45, the thick dark ghost zig-zag is drawn over the hairline-thin orange SGD trail, and the two get tangled in a small cluster around the minimum. It is hard to tell the SGD jitter cloud from the ghost's oscillation. The 'SGD' label floats away from the orange ball, which is half hidden inside the translucent ghost.

The host hid the gradient arrow because its true-scale length (0.363) is shorter than its head size. This is disclosed. Consider a thinner arrow head so short arrows still show. The low end of the learning rate and the batch-size extremes (1, 64) were not sampled.
From the side angle too, the thick dark ghost trail lies over the orange SGD trail and hides most of the noisy path.
The SGD trail is very thin compared with the ghost trail. It shows here, but it reads like a hairline.
